title: Want, need, can, must
description: Say what you want, what you have to do, what you can and cannot do, and what is allowed.

guide.title: Wanting a thing: dative + beku
guide.text:
'I want water' is ನನಗೆ ನೀರು ಬೇಕು (nanage neeru beku), literally 'to-me water is-wanted'. The person who wants is in the dative (nanage, nimage, avanige, avalige, avarige, namage), the thing wanted is the subject, and ಬೇಕು (beku) never changes.

beku covers both 'want' and 'need'.

Negative: ಬೇಡ (beda) - nanage beda, 'I don't want (it)'. A softer 'I don't need it' is ಬೇಕಾಗಿಲ್ಲ (bekaagilla).
Question: ಬೇಕಾ? (bekaa?) - nimage enu beku? 'what do you want?'; neeru bekaa? 'do you want water?'
Past: ಬೇಕಿತ್ತು (bekittu) 'wanted, was needed' - also a polite way to ask in a shop: nanage ondu pen bekittu, 'I was wanting a pen'.

This 'dative subject' pattern - the person in the dative, the feeling or thing as subject - is one of the keys to Kannada. You will meet it again with knowing, liking, having, being hungry and being ill.

examples.english: I wanted a pen. / I'd like a pen.

guide.title: Having to do something: verb + -abeku
guide.text:
Attach beku to a verb stem with a linking -a- and you get 'must, have to, need to, should': ಹೋಗಬೇಕು (hogabeku) must go; ಮಾಡಬೇಕು (maadabeku) must do; ಬರಬೇಕು (barabeku) must come; ತಿನ್ನಬೇಕು (tinnabeku) must eat; ನೋಡಬೇಕು (nodabeku) must see; ಕೊಡಬೇಕು (kodabeku) must give; ಇರಬೇಕು (irabeku) must be. Verbs in -i and -e insert y: kudiyabeku (must drink), iliyabeku (must get down).

The form is the same for every person. The person is usually in the plain form (naanu hogabeku); with the dative (nanage hogabeku) the sense leans towards 'I want to go'.

Stronger: insert the emphatic -e: ಬರಲೇಬೇಕು (baralebeku) 'really must come'.

Negatives - three different meanings:
needn't: ಬರಬೇಕಾಗಿಲ್ಲ (barabekaagilla), 'there is no need to come'.
don't (command): ಬರಬೇಡಿ (barabedi).
must not, shouldn't: ಬರಬಾರದು (barabaaradu).

Past: ಹೋಗಬೇಕಿತ್ತು (hogabekittu) 'had to go / should have gone'.

examples.english: You must not take photos here.

guide.title: Can: knowing how (barutte) and being able (aagutte)
guide.text:
Kannada separates two kinds of 'can'.

A skill you have learned 'comes to you': dative + skill + ಬರುತ್ತೆ (barutte). nanage kannada barutte, 'I can speak Kannada (Kannada comes to me)'. With a verb, use the -oke form: nanage eejoke barutte, 'I know how to swim'. Negative: ಬರಲ್ಲ (baralla). You will also hear barutte pronounced baratte.

Being able to do something on a given occasion 'happens for you': dative + verb in -oke + ಆಗುತ್ತೆ (aagutte). nanage baroke aagutte, 'I can come (it is possible for me)'. Negative: ಆಗಲ್ಲ (aagalla) - nanage baroke aagalla, 'I can't come'. Past: aaytu / aagalilla, 'managed to / couldn't'.

The -oke form ('to do, for doing') is made by adding -ಓಕೆ (-oke) to the stem: maadoke, hogoke, baroke, tinnoke, nodoke, odoke, kodoke; verbs in -i and -e insert y: kudiyoke, bareyoke. In written Kannada it is the infinitive in -alu: maadalu, baralu - so 'I can't come' is written nanage baralu aaguvudilla.

guide.title: May (permission) and liking
guide.text:
Permission and possibility use -ಅಬಹುದು (-abahudu), 'may, can': neevu illi kootkollabahudu, 'you may sit here'. To ask permission add -aa: ಬರಬಹುದಾ? (barabahudaa?) 'may I come?'. The refusal is -baaradu.

Liking is another dative pattern: dative + thing + ಇಷ್ಟ (ishta), 'liking'. nanage dose ishta, 'I like dosa'. Negative: ishta illa. To like doing something, use the -odu form of the verb (the spoken verbal noun, 'the doing'): nanage ododu ishta, 'I like reading'; nanage aduge maadodu ishta, 'I like cooking'.

phrases.note: beku = want or need. The e is long.
enaadaroo = anything at all. In speech: enaadroo (ಏನಾದ್ರೂ).
The inserted long -e- adds insistence - a warm way to invite someone.
Written: nanage kannada odalu baruttade (ಓದಲು ಬರುತ್ತದೆ).
A polite way to ask a favour.

phrases.english: You must not take photos here.
phrases.note: foto tege = to take a photo.
The o of dose is long.
With the dative nanage the sense is 'I feel the need to'.
